lesson.title: One Point Per Line: The Vertical Line Test
lesson.summary: A quick graphical check that turns the abstract definition of a function, one input and one output, into something you can verify just by looking at a graph.
lesson.body:
A function is a relation in which every input is matched with exactly one output. That single rule, one input, one output, is easy to state but not always easy to see just by staring at an equation or a graph, especially when a graph has a complicated shape. The vertical line test turns that abstract rule into something you can check with your eyes: draw a vertical line anywhere across the graph, and if it ever crosses the graph at more than one point, the relation is not a function, because that would mean one input (the x-value where the line sits) produces two or more outputs.

Why does a vertical line work as the test? Every point on a vertical line shares the same x-coordinate. If a vertical line at x = c touches the graph at two different points, say (c, 3) and (c, 7), then the input c is paired with both 3 and 7, which directly breaks the definition of a function. So sweeping a vertical line across the entire graph, checking every possible x-value at once, is really just checking the definition of a function visually instead of algebraically.

Consider the parabola y = x^2 - 4x + 3. To confirm it is a function, notice that for any x-value you substitute, the expression x^2 - 4x + 3 produces one and only one number, because arithmetic operations like squaring, multiplying, and subtracting always output a single result. Check x = 1: y = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0. Check x = 3: y = 9 - 12 + 3 = 0. Two different x-values can share the same y-value, that is allowed, but each individual x-value never splits into two y-values. No vertical line can cross this graph twice, so it passes the test.

Now compare that to the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25. Solve for y when x = 3: 9 + y^2 = 25, so y^2 = 16, and y = 4 or y = -4. A single input, x = 3, produces two outputs, 4 and -4. The vertical line x = 3 crosses the circle at (3, 4) and (3, -4), two points on the same vertical line, so the circle fails the test and is not a function of x.

A quick way to build intuition is to compare two closely related equations: y = sqrt(x) and x = y^2. The first, y = sqrt(x), is defined so that the radical symbol always returns the nonnegative root, so y = sqrt(9) = 3 only, never -3, and every vertical line touches this graph once. The second, x = y^2, is the same relationship solved the other way, and it fails the test: at x = 9, y^2 = 9 means y = 3 or y = -3, so the vertical line x = 9 crosses the sideways parabola twice. Swapping which variable is squared and which is isolated changes an equation from a function into a non-function, even though both describe the same underlying curve rotated onto its side.

This distinction matters because so much of algebra assumes you are working with a function: you cannot graph f(x) on a calculator, describe its domain and range cleanly, or later analyze it as discrete, continuous, or piecewise, unless it passes this basic check first. The vertical line test is the gatekeeper that every new graph in this course has to pass before the vocabulary of functions is allowed to apply to it.
